name: Figs
why_now: Mission figs run from late summer into fall, and August is when they turn serious. The best of them often arrive in the last two weeks of the month — earlier fruit can look right and still taste faintly green, because the tree wasn't finished with it. The window is short and worth waiting out. What you find at its peak was picked ripe and won't be available like this again until next year.
how_to_choose: The neck bends. A ripe fig hangs heavy and droops from its stem instead of standing straight out — this is the most reliable tell there is
Soft the whole way through, like a water balloon that's full. Not firm with a little give — properly soft
Fine cracks in the skin, and often a bead of syrup at the eye on the bottom. Both mean it's ready, not spoiled
Color follows the variety, not the ripeness. Mission figs go purple-black, but Kadota and Calimyrna are yellow-green when they're perfect. Don't reject a green fig — check its neck
A firm fig is a finished fig. If everything in the box is standing up straight, buy something else
buy_this_much: 1 pint for the week. Plan to eat most of them within two days of buying.
buying_note: This is the ingredient worth being difficult about. Lift the clamshell, tilt it, look at how the figs sit. If they're all upright and firm, put it back — a pint of underripe figs is expensive, faintly grassy, and cannot be rescued on the counter, because a fig does not ripen after it leaves the tree. It softens and eventually ferments; it never gets sweeter. The nectarines can carry the weekend plate.
price_note: Figs are briefly abundant in August and reasonably priced at farmers markets. Grocery store figs are available but are often picked early so they survive the trip — which is exactly the fruit that never comes good. The farmers market version is worth the detour this month.

flavor_paths.name: Nearly nothing
flavor_paths.description: Halved and eaten as they are. Salt if you want it.

flavor_paths.name: Sweet
flavor_paths.description: Sliced on yogurt with a little honey. That's breakfast.

flavor_paths.name: Savory
flavor_paths.description: With prosciutto, burrata, and arugula. The weekend plate.

weekday_uses: Halved on Greek yogurt in the morning
Eaten as a snack, ripe, over the sink
weekend_use: The weekend plate: halved figs, torn burrata, prosciutto, arugula, olive oil, and flaky salt. Eat with bread.
storage: Out of the clamshell, stem down on a plate in a single layer, on the counter for a day — two at most. Refrigerate only if you have to, and eat them soon after. Do not buy them expecting them to keep, and do not buy them expecting them to improve.
one_thing_to_learn: A fig isn't really a fruit. It's a flower turned inward — a hollow stem end lined with hundreds of tiny blossoms that never see daylight. That's why the rules are different from every other fruit in the basket. A peach or a nectarine keeps ripening after picking because it carries its own reserves; a fig is fed through its stem right up until the moment it's cut, and the instant that connection breaks, it is as sweet as it will ever be. Everything a fig has, it got on the tree. Your only job is to choose one the tree was finished with.
market_question: When were these picked — and which ones should I eat today?
